idiom_name: Data.define value operations + case/in pattern-matching interpreter
implementation_notes: `Data.define(:key)` (Ruby 3.2) gives frozen value objects with positional and keyword deconstruction, and `case ... in` (Ruby 3.0) matches on class plus keys - so the algebra is a handful of one-line Data classes and the interpreter is a single `case/in` expression, replacing a command hierarchy with an `execute` method. Without an `else` clause an unhandled operation raises `NoMatchingPatternError`, which is better than a silent fall-through but still a runtime check. Hash-based programs (`{op: :get, key: 'a'}`) are the lighter untyped alternative common in configuration-driven code, and mutable `Struct` is the older form to avoid; keep the class-with-behaviour form when operations genuinely own algorithms rather than describing effects.
code_sketch:
Get = Data.define(:key)
Put = Data.define(:key, :value)

def run(op, store)
  case op
  in Get[key:]          then store.read(key)
  in Put[key:, value:]  then store.write(key, value)
  end
end   # unhandled op => NoMatchingPatternError
pitfalls: Data instances are shallow-frozen: nested arrays/hashes can still change, so keep payloads immutable scalars.
Pattern matching needs Ruby 3.0+ and Data 3.2+; older runtimes must fall back to Hash plus case/when and lose the structural checks.
In hash patterns, `deconstruct_keys` only matches the listed keys, so a typo in a key name silently makes the pattern non-matching and the operation falls through to the next branch.
